Berkeley’s God

In my latest article at Postliberal Order, I discuss how the novel metaphysical assumptions that modern philosophy brought to the traditional project of establishing the existence and nature of God often either led to heterodoxy or greased the skids for atheism, using George Berkeley as a case study.

      I haven't read it either, but that puts me in the same boat as you so I think I am justified in answering.

      (1) While it would be very, painfully against good sense to ditch all of the science in the past 500 years merely because of some methodological problem exposed, there are clear disanalogies between science and philosophy for this issue. If you read Descartes' Discourse on the Method, for example, he explicitly represented himself to be starting from scratch, not correcting or building on the prior work of earlier thinkers. (a) Such a position would be reasonable (if analogous to doing the same to science) ONLY if the prior work had been fundamentally, systematically, and irreparably wrong-headed to the point where no real progress was even possible without starting from scratch. He nowhere establishes such a claim. (b) For those who don't agree - or at least don't see that it is probable - that the whole prior edifice was irreparably wrong-headed, they would be (at least procedurally) justified in ignoring his work just as he ignored all prior work. Regardless of how much time has now passed. To the extent that the works of Locke, Berkeley, Hume, Kant, Hegel, and Nietzsche built expressly to address DESCARTES (and successors), to that extent their works might be nearly as justifiably ignored. (To summarize: maybe they provided something worthwhile, but when it comes to the judgment call as to where to put most of my attention and effort, putting it on people who started by ignoring all of the past is often not very prudent.)

      (2) In fact, after such initial moderns as Descartes started, most of the following moderns themselves critiqued their predecessor moderns, often validly, to the extent that there are very few professors today who are uniquely allied with any single one of Descartes, Locke, Hume, Kant, etc., and (here's the rub) there is invariably 1001 different views on how to take, say, Hume and adjust / repair his arguments to overcome critiques of him: nobody in the modern era can AGREE on what would or would not represent a "fix" to Humean or Kantian errors to make a solid philosophy today. That is, the current situation in philosophy isn't like that of science, and it cannot be called "progress" in any analogous way. The best that can be said is that MANY of the errors of prior thinkers have been pointed out, but with a great deal of disagreement about even that.

      (3) Modern analytic philosophers who put a great deal of stock in "the perennial philosophy" of the Scholastics (not solely Thomists) do no simply ignore all of modern philosophy. It is more typical of them (and absolutely normal for Feser) to take critiques of the Scholastics into account, and also to accept some modern thinking elements as better than the Scholastics and try to incorporate such into their re-conditioning of scholastic philosophy. For example, the modern idea of subsidiarity is now typically explicitly incorporated into neo-Thomist political theory as a correction / refinement of some prior mistakes. But that has to be able to go both ways: while Augustine + Thomas indicated 4 important functions for economic modeling, Adam Smith tried to simplify the picture by modeling solely with supply and demand functions: later thinkers realized they had to add back in a 3rd, and later on the 4th, to make the picture work (See: Redeeming Economics, John Mueller).

      (1/2)
      Tony

      This is something I've wanted to hammer on for a while. Feser has this pet idea where he blames Horrible Early Modern Philosophers (Descartes most prominently) for deliberately and illegitimately choosing to reject Scholasticism for ulterior motives. But the vast majority of philosophers and historians of philosophy don't seem to agree, as can be seen by the fact that you don't see anyone except Feser making this kind of claim. It's more like a conspiracy theory than anything else. But let's address your points one by one.

      1. The claim that it is "unreasonable" for Descartes to try to build from scratch rather than relying on the Scholastics is absurd. You don't need to "refute" a prior metaphysics in order to propose a new one! That's ridiculous! Especially given that it's usually impossible to refute a metaphysics so decisively that it cannot be patched up or modified by someone who's motivated to want to keep it. We'd never learn anything if we followed your principles. Anyone can make up any metaphysics they want. The only thing we can do is to compare which of them is the most useful tool for understanding the world, which advantages one has over another, which paradoxes one is vulnerable to vs immune to, which ones better cohere with our scientific knowledge and/or common experience of reality, etc. The idea that you're not allowed to drop a prior metaphysics unless you've decisively refuted it is nonsense. You can do it simply because you're unsatisfied with it (say, with its inability to solve certain questions).

      In Descartes' case, he lays out his reasons for doing so pretty clearly - one, he wants certain knowledge rather than merely probable knowledge gained through sensation. He wants to be *absolutely* certain of his knowledge rather than merely pretty sure (the Scholastics believed that all knowledge came through the senses, which are inherently fallible).

      Two, as regards his rejection of substantial forms, he explicitly states (in his "Meteorology" as well as a January 1642 letter to Regius) that his reasons for ignoring them is because he finds them both useless and unnecessary as regards explaining natural phenomena. He doesn't explicitly reject them as false, but claims that we can make better progress in understanding the natural world through leaving them aside. And there is absolutely nothing wrong with him doing so. He does not need to prove that there are no substantial forms in order to decide to do this.

      Sure, every thinker great and small has been imperfect and has been critiqued by later writers. That's perfectly fine and normal. You are free to inquire into Thomism, Pythagoreanism, Platonism, Descartianism, Hobbesianism, Lockeanism, and countless others. Each of them can be and is critiqued and compared to each other, tested for which is the best on several metrics (conformity with known experience, internal coherence, logical rigor, explanatory power, etc). Severe deficiency in these fields is good reason to reject a metaphysics, in whole or in part. Most modern thinkers don't find Thomism very convincing because however internally coherent or rigorous it is, it doesn't grapple well with experience and especially with modern scientific reality (try giving a Thomistic account of evolution, for instance!).

      And sure, if you want, you can say that morality has regressed or stagnated instead of progressing over the last 500 years. But the thing is, Thomistic morality is not easily separable from Thomistic metaphysics more generally. If the basic metaphysics is suspect or fails to explain reality well, then it is spurious to suggest that it explains morality well. Perhaps you could cobble together a Thomist moral framework with a modern physical framework, but that would not sit well together, and would require extensive argumentation as to why you're holding to principles in one area while denying or ignoring them in another.

      Sure, it's good to see that Neo-Thomists have adopted some modern ideas into their frameworks. And I'm sure there are *some* worthwhile ideas that can be salvaged from Scholasticism. But that's more like picking over a car for unrusted parts than taking it out and fixing it.

      Look, we could go back and forth all day, but at the end of it all my basic request is this: drop the conspiracy theories and the persecution complex. Just accept that your favorite philosophy fell out of a position of intellectual dominance for valid reasons and focus on trying to fix and promote it rather than complaining about that overthrow.

      Indeed, which is why we get many, TOO many to consider in depth, which is why we must prioritize and weed out the ones we are NOT going to delve into carefully. We need a filtering method.

      But in fact we tend to NOT do this for all proposals: for the most part, we tend to eliminate most proposals from serious consideration before considering them in depth, because on their face they have some feature that makes them (given our existing understanding) so improbable that they aren't worth our time. I don't bother to worry about the claims of the Flat-Earthers, as being not worth my time, (though I am perfectly happy a few people out there bother.) A brand new proposal has to situate itself in a way that merits my serious consideration, and flat out rejecting the whole of prior philosophy (without addressing it in detail) hits one of the standard filters for "probably not worth it". Doesn't make it wrong, of course. It might be quite right. But then, given the number of later moderns who rejected Descartes, it seems that he also didn't hit on a "certain" system. So...that's another filter reject.

      The idea that you're not allowed to drop a prior metaphysics unless you've decisively refuted it is nonsense.

      You're arguing against something I wasn't proposing. I was addressing the matter of getting others to decide to consider your proposal seriously, not whether you are allowed to propose it without first disproving the prior theories. Sure, you're allowed. And others are ALSO allowed to not bother to take you seriously, and you can't then insist that they're proceeding in bad faith or foolishly on that account. In science it is considered "bad form" to propose brand new models that completely reject prior models, without giving at least some reasons for rejecting prior models, like some shortcomings. This is a filter mechanism scientists (who are, each of them, limited humans) use. Why shouldn't it also work for philosophers proposing brand new complete systems?

And don't try to pivot into "well we also invented nukes and machine guns" - I know that, but all that I'm discussing here is the fact that advancement has indisputably been rapid, far more so than was possible under Scholasticism.

      "moral philosophy post Descartes is a shambles"

      I'm going to have to ask you to be more specific about what you mean. Do you mean that you think it is bad, morally bad? If so, isn't that your own subjective judgment? Or do you mean that it is disunified, in that there is little widespread agreement? In which case, why is that a problem? Morality is complicated. The world is complicated. You might long for a simpler world where there was one singular authority administering morality from on high, but that's again, nothing more than your preference. An admission that you are more comfortable being told what to think than thinking for yourself.

      "we (directly) experience OURSELVES operating with final causality"

      This is a muddle. We experience ourselves acting for purposes, of course. Whether you believe this is "illusion" or not, it doesn't require us to buy into the entire Thomistic Four Causes framework. We simply have purposes and are capable of acting on them. That mere fact doesn't establish anything beyond itself. In fact, it seems more plausible to suggest that, rather than "abandoning the obvious truth of final causes", the belief in final causes existing outside of us is actually the result of imposing our own way of thinking and action on the world, assuming it operates the way our minds do.

      ""forms" are indeed needed to explain our experience of intentional action and the resulting experiences of moral right and wrong, of justice and injustice."

      Why? Plenty of non-Thomist metaphysics exist that can explain the fact that humans act intentionally and have opinions about right and wrong. Nothing about intentional action requires one to believe in final causes. If you want to argue that it's *the best* explanation of such, then be my guest. And as for morality, there are also loads of alternative explanations of what it is, how we can know it, etc. Just on the atheist side, for instance, probably the most common view roots right and wrong in the subjective value judgments of human beings - say, "I do not want to be murdered, and since I have empathy, I understand that others also do not want to be murdered. So we should agree amongst ourselves to forbid murder because nobody wants it to happen." Or, even if the person does not have empathy, they may rationally recognize that a society which permits murder is one in which they are in turn more likely to be murdered, and so it is in their best interests to support the outlawing of murder. Yet another atheist may state that these principles *are* objective, grounded in realities about human biology and psychology. IE, "not being the kind of person who murders other people will make you happier, so you ought to not commit murder", or "living honestly rather than dishonestly will objectively lead to you feeling more satisfied with yourself". You may disagree with any or all of these ideas if you want, but my point is that there are plenty of ways to explain our moral feelings without appealing to forms.

    1. Edward FeserAugust 31, 2026 at 9:45 PM

      Hi Norm,

      Would you say that if our cognitive faculties were not oriented towards truth, something as clear as basic arithmetic 2+2=4 could reasonably be called into question,

      That’s an ambiguous question. Would 2 + 2 = 4 itself be called into question? No. Would our being justified in believing that proposition be called into question? Yes.

      is it the reliability of our cognitive faculties that ground mathematical truths ?

      No.

      Couldn't one say though that mathematical logic is true irrespective of the reliability of our cognitive faculties

      Yes, but what is at issue in the argument you refer to is how we could have access to them. Basically, you seem to be treating the issue as if it were about metaphysics (what is in fact the case) when it is about epistemology (how we could have access to what is the case).

      Why can't every approximation be taken as an individual shape in itself, why call it an imperfect triangle when it could just be in it's own category instead of "triangle"

      It depends on what we’re talking about. A triangle isn’t strictly a substance, but consider something that is, such as a dog. What we already independently know about dogs (their ordinary life habits and needs, the traits they exhibit when not interfered with or damaged, etc.) is what tells us that a dog that is missing a leg is an imperfect instance rather than its own kind of thing.

      Notice that none of this requires -- any more than Rosenberg’s own arguments do -- an appeal to introspection, phenomenology, etc. When Rosenberg gives you an argument, he gives you the premises (about the success of science or whatever) that he says you are already implicitly or explicitly committed to, and then tells you what conclusion he takes logically to follow from them. He doesn’t appeal to introspection of his phenomenal awareness, any more than Rosenberg does. Ross’s argument is not: “Here is how things seem to me introspectively, and how I assume they seem to the eliminativist too.” His argument is: “The eliminativist’s arguments, like everyone else’s, presuppose such-and-such patterns of formal reasoning; yet he is also committed to denying that anyone’s arguments, including his own, are of those or any other determine patterns. That is incoherent.” Here too the focus is on the arguments themselves, not on anyone’s introspective awareness of entertaining the arguments. Indeed, the emphasis is precisely on those aspects of an argument -- such as its formal validity or invalidity -- by reference to which we judge the way things seem to us introspectively (as in “Sure, it might seem that if all men are mortal and Socrates is mortal, then Socrates is a man, but that is in fact in invalid syllogism form”).
